extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic drama: choices about plot-structure, character, recognition, and the parts of tragedy to produce pity and fear. Focused on classical (Greek) tragedy construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise combined with causal necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events should come upon the audience by surprise while at the same time following as cause and effect; coincidences are most striking when they have an air of design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tragic wonder is heightened if incidents surprise us yet are the necessary or probable result of preceding actions (propter hoc not post hoc). Avoid mere accidental coincidences that feel arbitrary. Example: the statue of Mitys at Argos falling on his murderer—seems designed rather than random.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex plot (prefer complex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are either Simple or Complex. A Simple action is one continuous change of fortune without Reversal and without Recognition. A Complex action includes Reversal, Recognition, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A perfect tragedy should be arranged on the complex plan so that reversals/recognitions arise from the internal structure of the plot and follow by probability or necessity. Complex plots are capable of producing pity and fear more effectively than simple plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of the Situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject always to the rule of probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversal should be motivated by the plot (not arbitrary). Examples: in Oedipus a messenger who intends to cheer produces the opposite effect; in Lynceus the intended slayer ends up slain. Reversal combined with recognition is especially powerful for producing pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition (anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between the persons destined to good or bad fortune; best when coincident with Reversal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recognition most intimately connected with plot is recognition of persons. Recognition combined with Reversal produces pity or fear, and thus is the heart of Tragedy. Recognitions should arise from the plot's internal dynamics rather than arbitrary devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene of Suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: The Scene of Suffering is a destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily agony, wounds, and the like).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include scenes of suffering as one of the parts that contribute to tragic effect, but ensure they fit the plot's internal necessity/probability rather than being gratuitous spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Tragedy's quantitative parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts: Prologue, Episode, Exode, Choric song (Parode and Stasimon); some plays also include songs of actors and the Commos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know the functions: Prologue precedes the Parode; Episode lies between complete choric songs; Exode has no choric song after it; Parode is the Chorus's first utterance; Stasimon is a choric ode without certain metric feet; Commos is a joint lament of Chorus and actors. Use these divisions appropriately when structuring a play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to excite pity and fear (choice of subject)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy should imitate actions that excite pity and fear; the change of fortune should not be the spectacle of a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity, nor the rise of a bad man to good, nor merely the downfall of an utter villain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best protagonists are men of mixed character—renowned and prosperous, not eminently good nor wholly bad—whose misfortune comes from error or frailty (hamartia). Such a figure arouses pity (unmerited misfortune) and fear (the misfortune of a man like ourselves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Single issue and direction of change
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single in its issue and the change of fortune should be from good to bad (not from bad to good).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid double-threaded plots with opposite catastrophes when seeking the highest tragic effect. The downfall should result from error, not vice. The theatre's practice supports single-issue tragic plots (e.g., Oedipus, Orestes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer inner-structure causes over spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear and pity are best aroused by the inner structure of the piece rather than by spectacular means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A superior poet produces horror and pity even in a purely aural telling of the tale; reliance on spectacle creates monstrous impressions and is less artistic. Spectacle can be used as a concomitant but should not substitute for properly constructed incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relationships (kinship/friendship) to heighten pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions capable of producing terror or pity should occur between persons who are friends, enemies, or indifferent—but incidents between those near or dear (kin, family) are most effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An enemy killing an enemy excites little pity; kin-slaying or threatened kin-slaying (father/son, mother/son, brother/brother) is the material poets should look for, and traditional legends should be handled with invention and skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of perpetration and their effects (ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deed may be done wittingly with knowledge, done in ignorance with discovery afterwards (best), be about to be done knowing then not done (worst), or be discovered before irreparable action is taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best effect: deed perpetrated in ignorance with later discovery (startling, no initial shock). Worst: a character is about to commit the deed knowing the relation and then refrains—shocking but not tragic since no disaster follows. Other variations occur but should be chosen for their tragic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character aims: goodness, propriety, verisimilitude, consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: In respect of Character the poet should aim at four things: first, goodness; second, propriety (appropriate traits); third, truth to life (verisimilitude); fourth, consistency (even if inconsistent, be consistently inconsistent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodness: moral purpose expressed in speech/action. Propriety: traits appropriate to class/sex/status. Truth to life: believable behavior distinct from mere moral labels. Consistency: characters must behave in ways consistent with their established nature; avoid motiveless degradation or incoherent shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Events and character must follow necessity or probability; avoid Deus ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Both complication and unravelling of the plot must arise out of the plot itself by necessary or probable sequence; irrational elements should be excluded or placed outside the action. The Deus ex Machina must not be used to resolve what should follow from the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deus ex Machina may be employed only for events external to the drama (antecedent or subsequent events beyond human knowledge). Keep all essential turns within the realm of believable causation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory appeals are concomitants, not essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to the senses (spectacle, music, etc.) are concomitants of poetry and can be used but are not among the essentials of tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is room for error in sensory appeals; they should support, not replace, the imitation that produces pity and fear. For further detail, consult treatises on those arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by signs and tokens (least artistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition may occur by congenital signs (birthmarks, emblems) or acquired bodily marks or external tokens (scars, necklaces, little ark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such token-based recognitions are the common and least artistic form (formal proofs are less artistic). They can be used but are lower in artfulness than recognitions arising from incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by a turn of incident (better)
rubrics_metrics.description: A better kind of recognition is that which comes about by a turn of incident (e.g., the Bath Scene in the Odyssey).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mode integrates recognition into the plot's causal flow and is therefore more artistic and satisfying than token-based proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition invented by the poet (speech-declarations) is inelegant
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognitions invented at will by the poet—where a character simply declares the identity because the poet wants it—are lacking in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contrived self-revelations (e.g., Orestes gratuitously saying he is Orestes) that do not naturally follow from the plot; they are akin to the faults of token-recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by memory/evoked feeling (most artistic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition depending on memory when the sight or sound of some object awakens feeling (e.g., seeing a picture or hearing a song) produces recognition by reminiscence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This kind (evoked memory or feeling) is an artistic form of recognition: it arises from associative memory and integrates emotion and plot (examples: heroes weeping on seeing a picture or hearing a lay which recalls the past).
